t: Introduction: aim and outline of the session
n: In this session we will consider the examination of living persons. The examination of living persons is one of the most frequently performed examinations in practice, and is ordered in criminal, civil and administrative cases. Here is the outline of chapter 12. First 12.1, bodily injuries. Then 12.2, the state of health, simulation, aggravation, dissimulation, artificial diseases and self-mutilation. Next 12.3, sexual conditions. Section 12.4 is devoted to sexual offences: rape, sodomy, indecent acts, sexually transmitted diseases and infection with HIV, that is, human immunodeficiency virus. Finally, 12.5, the procedure for conducting the examination. The general algorithm begins with studying the circumstances of the event and ends with drawing up the expert's conclusion, and it consists of 6 stages.

t: When an examination of living persons is ordered
n: Now we will see when an examination of living persons is ordered. The examination is ordered in the prescribed cases in criminal, civil and administrative matters. It is carried out in the departments of forensic medical institutions; sometimes also in treatment facilities that have the necessary conditions. The types of examination include bodily injuries, sexual conditions, sexual offences, simulation and artificial disease, as well as state of health and age. The examination of sexual conditions also includes determining virginity, pregnancy, previous childbirth and abortion. In bodily injuries, the nature of the injury and the degree of severity are determined.

t: Questions resolved in the examination of bodily injuries
n: In the examination of bodily injuries, the expert resolves a number of questions. He determines the type, location and features of the injuries, and the kind of weapon or means that inflicted the injury. In addition, the mechanism of occurrence of the injury and the age of the injury are established. Then the degree of severity is determined, with the qualifying feature indicated. All this information must be recorded in the expert's conclusion. Attention: the forensic severity of an injury is not equal to its clinical severity. Their purposes and criteria differ, so the results may not coincide.

We turn to the legal classification of bodily injuries. According to the Criminal Code, bodily injuries are divided into grievous, moderate and slight. Under Article 104, danger to life, loss of an organ, mental disorder and disfigurement are regarded as grievous injury. Article 105 gives the features of moderate injury, and Article 109 gives the features of two kinds of slight injury. On the severity scale, impairment of up to 6 days is slight, 6–21 days is slight short-term, and more than 21 days is moderate. Danger to life, or a loss of 33 per cent or more, corresponds to grievous injury.

t: Criteria for determining the degree of severity (table 12.1)
n: Table 12.1 gives the criteria for determining the degree of severity. The criteria are as follows: danger to life, duration of impairment, working capacity, loss of an organ, mental disorder and disfigurement. One criterion alone is sufficient. If there are several criteria, the one corresponding to the more severe degree is adopted. According to the table, danger to life or a loss of 33 per cent or more indicates grievous injury. A loss of 10–33 per cent or impairment of more than 21 days corresponds to moderate injury. If short-term impairment is up to 10 per cent or 6–21 days, the injury is slight; simple impairment of up to 6 days is also slight. Attention: forensic and clinical assessments are not the same.

t: The criterion of danger to life
n: Let us speak about the criterion of danger to life. An injury that at the time of infliction directly threatens a person's life, or creates a life-threatening condition, is considered dangerous to life. The list includes wounds penetrating the skull, chest and abdominal cavities, fractures of the skull and cervical vertebrae, injuries to large blood vessels, and severe burns. Conditions such as severe shock, grade II–III coma, massive blood loss, sepsis, peritonitis and embolism are also considered life-threatening. Attention: the threat must be directly connected with the injury, not accidental. Even if medical assistance removes the threat, the assessment does not change.

t: Permanent loss of general working capacity
n: Now the permanent loss of general working capacity. General capacity means self-care and simple work, while professional capacity refers to occupational activity. In assessing severity, only general capacity is taken. Impairment exceeding 120 days is regarded as conditionally permanent loss, and its percentage is determined by a special table. In grievous injury the loss is 33 per cent or more, in moderate injury 10–33 per cent, and in slight injury up to 10 per cent. Fractures of the humerus, femur and tibia lead to a loss of more than a third, that is, they are considered grievous injury.

The duration of health impairment is the most frequently used criterion; it denotes a disturbance of organ function associated with temporary incapacity for work. The duration is set in days on the basis of objective medical data, and doctors must justify the length of treatment. The limits in days are as follows: up to 6 days, slight; 6–21 days, slight, short impairment; more than 21 days, moderate. Remember: the duration of impairment is not equal to the duration of treatment. Absence of treatment does not negate impairment, and a delay in treatment is not taken into account.

The first quick question concerns classification and limits. How is an injury assessed if the impairment is up to 6 days? Answer: slight bodily injury. Second question: to which category does a 21-day impairment belong? Answer: slight injury with short-term impairment of health; more than 21 days is moderate. Third question: at what percentage is permanent loss grievous? Answer: not less than 33 per cent; 10–33 per cent is moderate, up to 10 per cent is slight. Attention: there is a risk of error. Days denote temporary impairment, while percentages denote permanent loss; do not mix them up.

t: Loss of vision, speech and hearing
n: Now the loss of vision, speech and hearing. Permanent complete blindness in both eyes, or visual acuity of 0.04 and below, is considered grievous bodily injury. Loss of one healthy eye is also grievous injury; if a blind eye is lost, the assessment is made by the duration of health impairment. As to speech, if the tongue is lost completely or by half, the injury is considered grievous. For hearing there is a difference. Attention: complete deafness in both ears is grievous injury; if hearing is lost in only one ear, it is moderate injury.

t: Loss of an organ and of reproductive capacity
n: We shall look at the loss of an organ and of reproductive capacity. Loss of an arm or leg means separation from the body or permanent loss of function, that is, paralysis. Loss of a hand or foot is equated with them. An injury that led to loss of an organ or function is considered grievous bodily injury; the loss of one testicle, ovary or kidney also belongs here. Reproductive capacity in a man includes sexual intercourse and fertilisation, and in a woman sexual intercourse, conception, carrying a fetus and childbirth. If, as a result of injury, a condition arises that prevents these functions from being performed, reproductive capacity is considered lost.

The criterion of termination of pregnancy. Termination of pregnancy means miscarriage, intrauterine death of the fetus or premature birth regardless of the term; such an injury is considered grievous. The criterion is applied only when termination after trauma ends in the birth of a dead child, or a live but non-viable one. The termination must be directly connected with the injury. It must not be related to diseases preceding the injury, or to individual characteristics of the woman and fetus. If a viable live child is born, or an ectopic pregnancy is terminated, severity is determined by other criteria.

On mental disorder and indelible disfigurement. It is established whether a mental disorder is present, that it did not exist before the injury, and that it is related to the event. Only if the injury and the mental disorder are in direct causal connection is the injury assessed as grievous. In this, a forensic psychiatrist or psychiatrist determines the connection of the disorder with the trauma, and in case of doubt a neurologist and neurosurgeon exclude another cause of the disease. In disfigurement the mark must be indelible, that is, not disappearing spontaneously or with conservative treatment, and requiring plastic surgery. The property of being erasable is determined by a cosmetologist or plastic surgeon, while the court decides whether disfigurement exists.

t: Rules of assessment with several criteria and multiple injuries
n: Now the rules of assessment with several criteria and multiple injuries. In determining severity, the presence of one medical criterion is sufficient. If there was a previous disease or defect, only consequences causally connected with the new injury are taken into account. Deterioration caused by age, disease or a defect in medical care is not taken into account in assessing severity. If several criteria apply, the assessment is made by the more severe one. For a set of mutually aggravating injuries in one event, a single overall assessment is given. Each of the injuries inflicted at different times is assessed separately. If the essence or outcome is uncertain, severity is not determined.

t: Case analysis 1: assessing the severity of a bodily injury
n: First case analysis: assessing the severity of a bodily injury. The situation is as follows: the victim, who was healthy before the injury, lost the sight of one eye after the trauma. The health impairment lasts more than 6 days but does not exceed 21 days. Question: by which criterion and to which degree is severity determined? Why is the duration of impairment alone not chosen? The direction is as follows: complete loss of vision in one eye causes a loss of more than a third of working capacity. The more severe criterion is chosen, and the injury is assessed as grievous. Attention: clinical severity is not equal to forensic severity; the criterion rests only on general working capacity.

t: Determining the state of health and simulation
n: Now the topic of determining the state of health and simulation. The examination is ordered when a person fails to appear before the court or investigator because of illness, when a prisoner refuses to work, when execution of a sentence is deferred, and in evasion of military service. It is carried out by a commission, with the participation of clinical specialists. Medical documents are studied and, if necessary, the person is examined in hospital. Simulation is when a healthy person presents a non-existent illness as real. In this, subjective and objective signs of the disease may be displayed. To identify a simulator, he must be observed for a long time. Some examinations are carried out without warning, suddenly, repeatedly. Until a diagnosis is made, no treatment is prescribed.

Let us compare aggravation and dissimulation with simulation. Simulation is presenting a non-existent illness as real, with the aim of avoiding punishment or military service. In aggravation an existing illness is presented as more severe; subjective signs are more often exaggerated, and treatment is refused. It is analysed whether they correspond to objective findings. Dissimulation is the opposite of simulation: an illness or injury is concealed, for example by a driver, pilot or diver. It occurs less often and is always committed intentionally. In all three cases the examination is carried out by a commission, with the participation of clinical specialists; inpatient observation is often needed.

The second quick question concerns the types of simulation. First question: if a healthy person presents a non-existent illness as real, what is this condition called? Answer: simulation. Second question: if the signs of a genuine illness are exaggerated or treatment is not accepted, what is this? Answer: aggravation. Third question: if a pilot or driver conceals an illness, what is this? Answer: dissimulation. Attention: there is a risk of error; simulation is not equal to dissimulation. The first displays an illness, while the second conceals it.

Now artificial diseases. On the skin and under the skin, artificial swelling, tumour, abscess, phlegmon and dermatitis are produced. Tight binding or repeated light blows lead to swelling, and injecting paraffin or Vaseline under the skin leads to a tumour. Artificial diseases of the internal organs are rare. A laxative or soap causes acute gastroenteritis, a large amount of table salt causes nephrosonephritis, and substances such as ephedrine cause signs of hypertensive disease. In the eye, dust or acid causes conjunctivitis; in the ear a foreign body is introduced and the tympanic membrane is perforated. Artificial prolapse of the rectum leaves an injury in the anal region.

We continue with artificial diseases. In the eye, rubbing, dust, sand, acid or alkali cause conjunctivitis and keratitis. In the ear, a foreign body is introduced into the external auditory canal, and the tympanic membrane is perforated with a piercing object. Attention: in rectal prolapse induced with a bag of peas, unlike true prolapse, injuries are found on the mucous membrane and in the anal region. That is, the location of the injuries helps distinguish an artificial condition from a true disease.

t: Self-mutilation and signs of self-inflicted injury
n: Self-mutilation and signs of self-inflicted injury. Self-mutilation is the deliberate infliction of injury on oneself; it is most often done to avoid military service. The injury is most often inflicted by the person himself, and rarely by another person by agreement. The signs of self-inflicted injury are as follows. Location: an area accessible to the hand, mainly the palm. Weapon: sharp or firearm, sometimes a blunt object. Wounds: several superficial wounds are found nearby. In amputation, cutting at different levels is observed, whereas in an accident it is at one level. In an investigative experiment, the person's statement and the positions of the person and the weapon are checked under conditions close to the event.

Second case analysis: suspected self-mutilation. A hypothetical situation: a conscript explains an injury to the palm as an accident at work. On examination, on the left hand near the main injury, several superficial stab-incised wounds and amputation of fingers at different levels were found. Question: which of these signs are characteristic of self-inflicted injury, and what additional examination will the expert recommend? Compare the signs you saw on the previous slide with this situation.

On determination of sex and hermaphroditism. If doubt arises about sex, for example in issuing documents, in marriage, alimony or an investigation, an examination to determine sex is ordered. Hermaphroditism is the presence of sexual organs characteristic of both sexes at the same time. True and false types are distinguished. In true hermaphroditism, male and female glands are present together. In false hermaphroditism, the external features resemble male or female: in the false male there is a scrotum, spermatogenesis is observed, and the external features are female; in the false female there is an ovary, oogenesis is observed, and the external features are male. The examination studies the history, medical documents, anthropometry, laboratory data and the chromosomes in leukocytes.

Determination of sexual maturity. Sexual maturity is the level of development that allows sexual life without harm to health; in girls it includes intercourse, pregnancy, childbirth and nursing. Usually, up to the age of 14, a person is considered sexually immature. The question arises from age 14 up to the age of marriage. In the Criminal Code, the ages of responsibility are set at 14, 16 and 18. In girls, standing height is at least 150 cm, sitting height 80 cm. Pelvic dimensions: interspinous 26–27, intercristal 29, external conjugate 17–18 cm. The indices are relative. At maturity the body of the uterus makes up two thirds of it, and the cervix one third. Otherwise the uterus cannot carry a fetus to term.

Virginity and the hymen. Virginity is determined mainly by the anatomical integrity of the hymen. The hymen is a fold of the vaginal mucous membrane, consisting of a base, a free edge and an opening. There may be several openings or none. The forms of the hymen are distinguished by frequency of occurrence. Annular and semilunar forms, and also the tubular form, are usual. Lobed, spiral and toothed forms are unusual. Bivalve, septate and imperforate forms are very rare. At first intercourse defloration occurs; in an elastic, low hymen with notches it may not occur.

t: Stages of healing of a hymenal injury
n: Stages of healing of a hymenal injury. In the first days the edges bleed, with swelling and clots. Later the swelling decreases and a whitish coating appears. At the end of the 1st week it is covered with granulation tissue. From the end of the 2nd week to the 3rd week a scar forms. After three weeks it is no longer possible to determine the age of the tear; the age is established only in the first weeks. Attention: a tear is not equal to a natural notch. A tear is most often between the 5 and 7 o'clock positions, whereas a notch does not reach the base. In case of doubt, a forensic medical expert should be consulted as soon as possible, since semen persists in the vagina for 3–5 days.

Determination of reproductive capacity. In a man, reproductive capacity denotes sexual intercourse and fertilisation, and in a woman, the ability to have intercourse, become pregnant and give birth. The cause of impotence may be a disease of the central nervous system, that is the CNS, a defect of the external organ, an endocrine disease or a neurotic reaction. Normally motile spermatozoa in the ejaculate confirm fertilising capacity; azoospermia, necrospermia and asthenospermia exclude it. In a woman, vaginal atresia, vaginismus, a narrow pelvis, a disease of the genital organs or an operation present an obstacle. The examination is carried out with the participation of clinicians.

t: Determination of pregnancy, childbirth and abortion
n: Determination of pregnancy, childbirth and abortion. In pregnancy there is no menstruation and the breast enlarges; reliable signs are the fetal heartbeat and ultrasound data. A trace of childbirth is a slit-like external os of the cervix. Abortion means termination of pregnancy before 22 weeks. It is medical or criminal; for criminal abortion there is liability under Article 114 of the Criminal Code. Methods of criminal abortion are mechanical, chemical, thermal and, rarely, electric current. Consequences: air embolism, shock, bleeding, perforation, poisoning and infection; it can lead to death.

The third quick question concerns sexual conditions. First question: up to what age is a person considered sexually immature? Answer: usually those under 14 years of age are regarded as immature. Second question: how long does semen persist in the vagina? Answer: usually 3–5 days, so the sooner the sample is taken, the more reliable the result. Third question: up to what time can the age of a violation of hymenal integrity be determined? Answer: in the first weeks; after three weeks this question cannot be resolved. Fourth question: up to what term of pregnancy is its termination regarded as abortion? Answer: up to 22 weeks; medical abortion at the woman's wish is carried out up to 12 weeks.

t: Case analysis 3: virginity and sexual maturity
n: Third case analysis: virginity and sexual maturity. Situation: there is a suspicion that a prepubertal girl has had sexual intercourse. The parents have approached an ordinary doctor and are asking what to do. First question: to which specialist and when should she be sent? Answer: as soon as possible to a forensic medical expert, not to an obstetrician-gynaecologist. Second question: how does a tear in the hymen differ from a natural notch? A tear is most often in the lower segment, between the 5 and 7 o'clock positions, and reaches the base. Attention: there is a risk of error! A violation of hymenal integrity does not come from sexual intercourse alone; sometimes defloration does not even occur in intercourse.

Now sexual offences, the first being rape. Under Article 118, this is sexual intercourse against the victim's will, using violence, threat, or taking advantage of her helplessness. Helplessness is associated with mental illness, intoxication, age or a defect. Before the examination, the decision, the record and the medical documents are studied, then the interview is conducted and the gynaecological history taken. Remember: a threat leaves no objective signs. Traces of violence are bruises and abrasions, found most often on the inner surface of the thigh and on the genitalia.

We continue with rape. There may be a tear of the hymen and haemorrhages in the vagina and perineum. A smear is taken from inside the vagina and imprints from the external regions. This is done faster, because over time the chance of finding spermatozoa decreases. Suspects are also examined. That is, the expert examines not only the victim but also the suspects, so that the traces on both sides can be compared.

Sodomy and indecent acts. Under Article 120, sexual intercourse of a man with a man without violence is sodomy; both participants bear liability. Indecent acts are obscene acts against persons under 16, provided for in Article 129; no traces may remain. In the active participant, traces are on the penis and the pubic region: blood, hair, faeces, an oily substance; if violence is involved, liability arises under Article 119. In the passive participant, semen, hair and an oily substance are found in the anus and rectum; if there was violence, he is the victim. Attention: diseases such as proctitis and haemorrhoids may be mistakenly interpreted as a sign of passive sodomy.

t: Sexually transmitted diseases, spread of HIV/AIDS
n: On sexually transmitted diseases and the spread of HIV and AIDS. Attention: rape is a crime against sexual freedom. Infection with a sexually transmitted disease and with HIV, that is, human immunodeficiency virus, is considered a crime dangerous to life or health. Under Article 113, knowingly infecting with, or placing at risk of, a sexually transmitted disease or HIV infection or AIDS is punishable. That is, these crimes are directed at different legal objects, so they must be distinguished from one another.

t: Sexually transmitted diseases, spread of HIV/AIDS (continued)
n: We continue with sexually transmitted diseases and the spread of HIV and AIDS. HIV infection through improper performance of official duties is also provided for in this article; this situation is more often related to the activity of medical staff. A dermatovenerologist and an AIDS specialist take part in the examination. The source of infection and the stage of the disease are studied, and a person in a late stage is regarded as a subject.

t: Case analysis 4: examination in a sexual offence
n: Fourth case analysis: examination in a sexual offence. Situation: suspected rape; the victim is brought in with bruises and abrasions on the inner surface of the thigh and in the genital region. A smear is taken from inside the vagina, and imprints from the pubis, perineum and thighs. Semen usually persists in the vagina for 3–5 days, and with delay the chance of finding it decreases. The suspect is also examined: traces of a struggle may be found, that is bruises, abrasions and bites, as well as blood and hair belonging to the woman on the penis and pubis. Question: why can sampling not be delayed, and what is taken to the laboratory at the examination of the suspect?

t: Procedure for conducting the examination: general algorithm
n: Now the general algorithm of the procedure for conducting the examination. The legal codes, the Law on Forensic Expertise and the requirements of the Instruction are taken as the basis. The procedure and methodology depend on the nature of the event and the tasks of the examination; each type has its own features. The algorithm consists of six stages: the data of the decision or ruling, the circumstances of the event, medical documents, interview of the person, examination with the aid of instruments, additional laboratory and consultative examination, then the final document, that is, the expert's conclusion. Attention: the conclusion is drawn up at the very end; before the examination, the circumstances and medical documents are studied.

On documents, interview, examination and participants. Identity is confirmed by a passport, military ID or birth certificate. In sexual conditions and offences, two photographs are also provided. The originals of medical documents are provided; the person who ordered the examination is responsible for their reliability. In the interview it is asked when, where, by whom, with what and how many times the injury was inflicted. Injuries are photographed only with the person's permission. When a person of the other sex is examined undressed, the investigator leaves the room.

We conclude the topic of documents, interview, examination and participants. Minors are examined in the presence of a parent or teacher, and persons lacking legal capacity in the presence of a legal representative. The examination of persons undergoing treatment is carried out in the presence of the attending doctor, if their state of health permits.

In conclusion, let us repeat the key principles. The procedure is specific to each type, but the general algorithm is one: circumstances, documents, interview, examination, additional examination, conclusion. Attention: the original of the medical documents is required, not a copy; photographing is possible only with the person's permission. Studying the documents in advance determines what to pay attention to at the interview and examination; this is especially important in assessing the initial state of an injury. Test yourself: list the stages of the algorithm. How many photographs are needed in the examination of sexual conditions? In whose presence is a minor's examination conducted?
